City placement depends on your plan for the game. Try to go for luxury resources if you feel you'll be growing a large empire, as you'll need as much happiness as you can get. Go for iron if anticipate taking the military route. Iron is particularly important if you think you'll need a navy, as frigates require iron. Getting a coastal city is important on maps where you expect you'll be settling some cities on other continents/islands. Rivers are excellent for production; you can build the water wheel early in the game, and the hydro plant later. You also get a city connection between cities on the same river. The game on easier modes recommends good locations for cities. In the early days you're safe enough accepting those recommendations, and later you'll know yourself where you want your cities to be. For example, the game will recommend locations based just on availability of resources and won't consider how the strategic placement of cities can be pretty useful. For example: you might place a city in order to prevent yourself from being isolated.

First, go into Single Player and then select Tutorial. Run through the tutorial once to get used to some of the basic concepts.

Then, go back to Single Player, and select Set up Game. - Leader-wise: There's no one best/easiest leader, as others have mentioned, but there are a few that are probably a little easier for the new player to work with. I'd suggest (and this is just a suggestion) you consider Augustus Caesar (Rome), Bismark (Germany), Oda Nobunaga (Japan), or Washington (America). Though, again, there are almost no wrong choices here. Usually, unless i'm doing something specific, I just roll with Random.
- Map Type: Continents. You get a good feel for both land and ocean exploration/warfare/etc.
- Map Size: I like Huge, but then again, I like big, sprawling empires. For a new user/first timer, Just swing Standard.
- Difficulty: Settler
- Game Pace: Standard.

Optionally, you can click "Advanced Setup" and there I might suggest clicking "No Barbarians" and "No Espionage". These are normally important parts of the game, but for your first time it might be a little easier without these on.

Also, go into the Game Options (hit Escape when your in game, or from the main menu). And under Game Options, set Advisor Level to "New to Civ". As it implies, this will adjust the advisors to give you more or less information.

Game time's vary a bit depending on your settings. I usually expect to spend about 10 hours or so on an individual game, but even that's approximate. Doesn't matter really. Finishing the game just means you'll start the next game. :) According to Steam, i'm up around 2200 hours just on Civ5.

I think that the Inca are a pretty good civ to start with. They don't have to deal with reduced movement in hills, pay no maintenance on roads build on hills, and their unique improvement (terrace farms) allows you to generate a TON of food with only a few tiles. Also, they're pretty much the only civ who can thrive in incredibly mountainous regions, which are unappetizing places to settle for just about every other civ in the game.

The length of a game depends on a lot of things. The larger the map/more AI civs, the longer it's going to take, obviously. IIRC a fast game is 250 turns, a normal game is 500, an epic game is 1000, and a marathon game is 1500. Unless you get an amazing start and totally roll your opponents, on normal game speed it usually takes at least 350 turns to win, usually more. A single game on normal (especially if there's a lot of war) can easily take like 8 hours.

A few tips/suggestions...

  1. Look into mods. There are SO many mods for Civ V, plenty of which are total game changers. New civs, the ability to create corporations, having cities rebel and secede if they get unhappy enough, making happiness localized to a specific city (rather than nationwide)...

  2. In the beginning turns of the game, food is the most important thing. Being able to work more tiles is invaluable. As you progress toward midgame, though, production becomes more important.

  3. Culture victory is really weird. Make sure understand all the aspects of it before you actually try it.

  4. Choosing the right policies for your situation can win or lose your game.

For your first Civ(s), there's some that are easier to learn different aspects of the game with:

Warfare: I like to use the Aztecs for learning how to fight. They get their unique warrior early in the game, and the constant culture bonus from killing opponents encourages practicing on some barbarians before taking down city-states and civs. The Japanese are more forgiving in the hands of a newer general, since their units don't suffer strength penalties at low hp, but they might teach you strategies that don't work for other civs.

Science: Korea and Babylon both rock a turtle-style game, where you slowly build up your cities and tech beyond anybody else's capabilities without trying to conquer most of the world.

Culture: Poland is one of the strongest civs in the game, partially because they're constantly getting new social policies. Tourism victories are so touchy that most of your early games should focus more on winning through science or domination.

As a side note- religions are fun, but you don't need to stress out if you're not founding one. Only a few civs benefit from founding a religion well enough to make it a "must-have." Caravans, however, are almost game-breakingly good. Just have a few sending food between your cities, and watch the population explode. Finally, make sure that you keep an eye on your civ's happiness. You don't have to run very high positive ratings (I'm normally 1-5), but negatives can completely destroy your empire.
